title: 2026 study provides new evidence that very young T. rex hatchlings fed early, but not hunting from birth
summary: The *Biology* paper’s fossil identification and bone structure support hatchlings that likely fed at an early stage, while tooth-wear evidence still leaves independent hunting from birth unproven and compatible with scavenging.

claims.text: A Biology paper titled "Hatchlings of Tyrannosaurus rex and the Evolution of Dinosaur Reproductive Strategies" was published in July 2026.

claims.text: The research centers on newly identified juvenile T. rex material from Saskatchewan's Frenchman Formation in Canada.

claims.text: The available coverage does not establish from independent primary reading whether the sample included more than one juvenile specimen or exactly how many fossils were analyzed.
The available coverage does not establish the full set of features used in the argument, beyond the foot bone and tooth wear references surfaced in secondary coverage.
The paper itself could not be directly read in this run, so the study’s methods and explicit limitations remain only partially verified here.
The Biology paper was published on 7 July 2026 in Biology 15(13):1090, with DOI 10.3390/biology15131090.

claims.text: Thomas R. Holtz Jr. argued in a reappraisal of the scavenging hypothesis that tyrannosaur anatomy does not justify treating T. rex as an obligate scavenger.

claims.text: Hone and Watabe showed that tyrannosaurid tooth marks on bones can record scavenging or postmortem carcass processing, so tooth traces alone do not prove a kill.

claims.text: Therrien et al. explicitly note that bite marks and feeding traces are difficult to distinguish from scavenging, and that juvenile tyrannosaur bite traces may reflect later-stage carcass consumption rather than live hunting.
